description:
Building contactless astronaut health monitoring: camera-based heart/stress tracking + NASA radiation data.

Muhammad Arham: CEO of OmniteX, built VitalSense (webcam HR/HRV/stress), AI + embedded.
Abdul Awwal: Electronics Eng, won all 4 robotics categories at SPEC’26 (NED).

We bring working tech and real hardware to validate it.

Looking for: someone who knows satellites, human exploration, ergonomics & human factors. Frontend/backend devs welcome too. Join us!
summary: CrewPulse is an offline-first health monitor that lets astronauts check their own health without waiting for Earth. Crew log their vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, SpO₂, stress and HRV) or take a 30-second webcam scan that measures heart rate on the laptop itself. Each reading turns green, amber or red only against a published guideline (AHA, ADA, CDC, NASA-STD-3001), and its source is shown on the card; with no source, it stays uncoloured. CrewPulse also learns each astronaut's own normal and flags "Unusual for you" when a reading stays outside it two days in a row. It adds NASA DONKI space-weather events, an estimated mission radiation dose, cabin CO₂ and air checks against NASA-STD-3001, and a 3D body map for logging symptoms. On a Mars mission, a message to Earth and its answer can take 40 minutes, and sometimes there is no link at all. CrewPulse works with no internet, explains every alert, and tells crew when to contact flight surgeons. It is decision support, never a diagnosis.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

CrewPulse is an offline-first self-health monitor for astronauts. It runs on one laptop with no internet connection.

- Log or scan: crew enter heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, SpO₂, self-reported stress and HRV (from a chest strap). Or they take a 30-second webcam scan that measures heart rate on the device, using the POS remote-photoplethysmography method (the colour of the forehead skin, filtered to 0.7–4 Hz, with the strongest frequency taken as the pulse). Face tracking runs in the browser, and only three colour averages per frame leave the page, never video. If the signal is weak, CrewPulse asks for a re-scan instead of showing a number.

- Colour only when cited: every reading turns green, amber or red only against a published guideline (American Heart Association, ADA, CDC, NASA-STD-3001), and the source is linked on the card. If no published threshold exists, the reading stays uncoloured. Guidance uses plain English: "consider a re-check" or "contact flight surgeons".

- Unusual for you: CrewPulse learns each astronaut's own 28-day baseline. When a reading stays more than 2 standard deviations away from it two days in a row, in the same direction, it flags "Unusual for you", even if the textbook calls the value normal. A 7-day trend slope shows slow drifts.

- Space environment: NASA DONKI space-weather events (solar flares, CMEs, geomagnetic storms, particle events) are cached for offline use. An estimated mission radiation dose comes from NASA's published ISS averages, clearly labelled as an estimate, and is shown against the 600 mSv career limit. Cabin CO₂, temperature and humidity are checked against NASA-STD-3001.

- Views: a 3D Earth dashboard whose satellites are your latest vitals, a 3D "vitals field" of 30 days of readings measured from your own baseline, trend charts, a Sun–Earth space-weather scene, a cabin log and a 3D body map for logging symptoms.

BENEFITS

- Works with no network, so crew can check themselves during communication delays or blackouts.

- Trustworthy: every colour can be traced to its source, and nothing is guessed.

- Personal: it catches changes that are normal for the population but unusual for that person.

- Few false alarms: requiring two days cuts them from about 1 in 22 checks to about 1 in 970 (assuming independent days), so crews don't learn to ignore alerts.

- Private: camera video never leaves the laptop.

INTENDED IMPACT

On a Mars mission, a question to Earth and its answer can take 40 minutes. CrewPulse gives crew an early, explainable signal of when to contact flight surgeons, covering NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. The same approach could help people in remote places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV, MediaPipe, httpx.

- Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite, three.js (react-three-fiber, drei), Recharts, and MediaPipe Tasks in a Web Worker for in-browser face tracking.

- Hardware: an ordinary laptop and its webcam; an oximeter for validation.

- Other: pytest (136 automated tests), GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for the public demo, Remotion and FFmpeg for the demo video, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

- Reuse: the signal-processing modules are adapted from Muhammad Arham's own open-source VitalSense project (MIT), used with the Karachi Local Lead's permission and attributed in the code.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Two independent checks on every reading: a cited guideline and the astronaut's own baseline.

- Heart rate from an ordinary webcam, with no extra hardware.

- Data shown as space instruments: vitals orbit a 3D Earth as satellites, and 30 days of readings form a 3D field of deviations from your own normal.

- NASA space-weather data and cabin-air checks sit alongside body vitals in one tool.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety and honesty: it is decision support, not a medical device; it never diagnoses, and it never invents a threshold.

- Scientific limits: no heart-rate variability or stress from the camera, because current evidence does not support it, so stress is self-reported. Camera heart rate is not yet validated against an oximeter, and it is known to be less accurate on darker skin, so the validation study needs a range of skin tones.

- Offline operation: fonts, API docs and NASA data are bundled or cached, and nothing needs the internet at runtime.

- Transparency: simulated data is always labelled "Simulated", and no machine learning is used, so a flight surgeon can check every rule.

- Privacy and usability: no video leaves the device, and the guide on screen covers lighting and distance for a good scan.
dataRefs: NASA CCMC DONKI - Space Weather Database (solar flares, CMEs, geomagnetic storms, SEP events)
NASA CCMC DONKI API (data source used by the app, cached for offline use)
NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 - Human Factors, Habitability and Environmental Health (cabin CO2, temperature, humidity limits)
NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 - Crew Health (600 mSv career radiation limit)
NASA - Space Faring: The Radiation Challenge (ISS dose averages for the mission-dose estimate)
NASA Human Research Program - 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight (problem framing)
projectRefs: American Heart Association - All About Heart Rate (resting heart rate 60-100 bpm)
2025 AHA/ACC High Blood Pressure Guideline (blood pressure bands)
American Diabetes Association - Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (glucose bands)
CDC - Definitions of Signs, Symptoms, and Conditions of Ill Travelers (fever 38 C)
Jones et al., SLEEP 2022 (short sleep under 5 hours)
Wang et al., Algorithmic Principles of Remote PPG, IEEE TBME 2017 (POS heart-rate method)
Bondarenko et al., Demographic bias in remote photoplethysmography datasets, npj Digital Medicine 2025
Fawzy et al., Racial and Ethnic Discrepancy in Pulse Oximetry, JAMA Internal Medicine 2022
VitalSense - own prior open-source work by Muhammad Arham, MIT (reused rPPG code, with Local Lead permission)
Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker (pre-trained face-tracking model, Apache-2.0)
React Three Fiber and Drei (3D components for React, MIT)
NumPy, SciPy and OpenCV (signal and image processing, BSD/Apache-2.0)
Fontsource - Archivo, Newsreader, JetBrains Mono fonts (SIL Open Font License)
Remotion and FFmpeg (editing the demo video)
Claude Code by Anthropic (AI coding assistant)
